title: KIDS Act
official_title: To protect children and teens online, empower parents and strengthen families, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Brett Guthrie (R-KY) and passed the House 267-117 on June 29, 2026; the bill creates FTC-enforced online-safety duties across obscenity sites, social platforms, video games, and AI chatbots, and now awaits Senate consideration.
summary: Sets new federal rules to protect people under 17 online. It requires adult-content sites to check whether users are minors, makes social platforms, video games, and AI chatbots add safety tools and parental controls, limits messaging features for young users, and orders several studies — all enforced by the Federal Trade Commission.
brief: Creates federal online-safety duties for adult sites, social platforms, video games, and AI chatbots aimed at users under 17, enforced by the FTC.

top_lines.headline: Age Checks for Adult Content Sites
subs: Sites where over one-third of material is harmful sexual content must verify users' age
Verification takes effect 1 year after enactment
Confirming you are not a minor is not enough to pass
Cannot be required to submit government-issued ID

top_lines.headline: Platform Safeguards and Parental Tools
subs: Covered platforms must give known minors safety controls, set most-protective by default
Must provide parental tools to manage settings, purchases, and screen time
Independent third-party audit required within 18 months, then annually

top_lines.headline: Messaging Limits for Young Users
subs: Bans disappearing (ephemeral) messaging features for known minors
Bans direct messaging for known users under 13
Parental direct-messaging controls required for teen users

top_lines.headline: AI Chatbot Rules
subs: Chatbots must disclose they are AI, not a person, to known minors
Must show suicide/crisis hotline resources when a minor raises suicide
Must advise a break after 3 continuous hours of use

top_lines.headline: Studies and FTC Enforcement
subs: Orders studies on social media, fentanyl access, chatbots, and safety tools
Violations treated as unfair or deceptive acts under the FTC Act
State attorneys general may sue on behalf of residents

sections.label: Section 1 — Short Title; Table of Contents

items.main: Names the Act the "Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act" or the "KIDS Act".
items.detail: Short-title and table-of-contents section — citation name and structure only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Defines terms used across the Act, including "minor" as an individual under age 17 and "chatbot," "design feature," and "personalized recommendation system."
items.detail: Ties several terms to existing law (artificial intelligence to 15 U.S.C. 9401; personal information and verifiable parental consent to the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act at 15 U.S.C. 6501). "Design feature" includes infinite scrolling, autoplay, push notifications, and personalized recommendation systems.

sections.label: Title I — Shielding Minors From Obscenity

items.main: Requires providers of "covered platforms" — sites where more than one-third of the material is sexual material harmful to minors — to adopt commercially available technology verification measures to identify minors and prevent them from accessing that material, beginning 1 year after enactment.
items.detail: Titled the "SCREEN Act." Providers must use an age-verification measure (a user's self-confirmation is not sufficient), give clear notice, limit retention of verification data, and maintain data-security practices. Providers may not be required to have users submit government-issued ID. The FTC must consult specified experts, and the Comptroller General must report to Congress within 3 years on effectiveness, compliance, privacy, and speech effects. States are preempted from requiring covered platforms to use technology verification measures.

sections.label: Title II — Addressing Harms to Minors on Online Platforms

items.main: Requires social-media-style "covered platforms" to maintain policies addressing enumerated harms to minors and to give known minors safety safeguards and parents parental tools, set to the most-protective level by default.
items.detail: Subtitle A ("Kids Online Safety Act") lists harms to address (threats of violence, sexual exploitation and abuse, drug/tobacco/gambling/alcohol activity, deceptive financial practices), requires reporting mechanisms with a response no later than 10 days, bars advertising illegal products to known minors, and requires an independent third-party audit within 18 months and annually thereafter (results to the FTC within 30 days, public report within 45 days). It states it does not impose a duty of care or require age gating.

items.main: Subtitle B ("Safe Messaging for Kids Act") bans ephemeral messaging features for known minors, bans direct messaging for known users under 13, and requires parental direct-messaging controls for teen users age 13 and up.
items.detail: Parental controls must, by default, alert parents to requests from unapproved contacts, let them approve or deny contacts, and let them disable messaging or hide a teen's profile. A rule of construction bars overriding strong encryption. Subtitle C ("SPY Kids Act") bars market or product research on known minors except to improve privacy, security, or safety, or as needed for legal compliance.

items.main: Requires online video game providers to give parents of known-minor users safeguards to limit communication with other players, enabled and set to the most protective level by default.
items.detail: Titled the "Safer GAMING Act." Providers must also give minors and parents easy-to-use tools to prevent a minor's profile from being recommended to non-minors, restrict purchases and financial transactions, and limit playing time, plus give clear notice when safeguards are in effect. States are preempted from regulating these communication tools and safeguards, except for general tort, contract, and consumer-protection law.

items.main: Sets rules for chatbot providers with respect to known-minor users, including a bar on falsely claiming the chatbot is a licensed professional and required disclosures.
items.detail: Titled the "SAFE BOTs Act." Providers must disclose the chatbot is an AI system and not a person at the first interaction and when a minor asks, and must provide suicide and crisis hotline resources when a minor raises suicide. Providers must maintain policies advising a break after 3 continuous hours of use and addressing minors' access to harmful sexual material, gambling, and restricted drugs, tobacco, or alcohol.

sections.label: Title V — Research, Education, and Best Practices

items.main: Orders multiple federal studies, education efforts, and a new partnership on protecting minors online.
items.detail: The FTC (with HHS) must study social media use by minors and report within 3 years; report on minors' access to fentanyl through social media within 1 year; and review industry safety tools, reporting within 3 years. HHS through NIH must run a 4-year longitudinal study on chatbots and minors' mental health. Section 522 amends the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act (15 U.S.C. 6551 et seq.) by striking sections 211 through 214 and 216 and inserting a new FTC public-awareness campaign, annual report for 10 years, and definitions. The AWARE Act directs FTC chatbot educational resources, and the Kids Internet Safety Partnership Act establishes a Commerce-led partnership that sunsets 5 years after it is established.

items.main: Sets enforcement, judicial review, rules of construction, severability, and the effective date for the Act.
items.detail: Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive acts under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the FTC Act and enforced by the FTC; state attorneys general may bring civil actions on behalf of residents after notice to the FTC. Constitutional challenges may be filed only in the D.C. Circuit, within 90 days of enactment. Rules of construction protect First Amendment-protected viewpoints, bar requiring decryption or weakening encryption, and bar altering section 230. Except as otherwise provided, the Act takes effect 1 year after enactment.

underreported.section: Section 522 — amendment to the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act
underreported.summary: Strikes sections 211 through 214 and 216 of the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act (15 U.S.C. 6551 et seq.) and replaces them with a new FTC public-awareness and education campaign, an annual report for 10 years, and definitions.
underreported.why_unreported: This part sits in Title V under an education heading, but the operative text repeals and rewrites parts of a separate existing statute rather than only adding new study or education activity.

underreported.summary: Each of Titles I through IV, and Subtitles B and C of Title II, bars states from maintaining or enforcing laws that conflict with or regulate the same subject as the relevant title, while preserving general tort, contract, product-liability, criminal, and consumer-protection law.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's stated purpose is protecting minors online, but multiple sections also limit state authority to regulate these areas — a preemption effect distinct from the safety mandates in the same titles.

underreported.section: Section 602 — judicial review in the D.C. Circuit
underreported.summary: Constitutional challenges to the Act may be filed only in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, which has exclusive jurisdiction, and only within 90 days of enactment for facial challenges.
underreported.why_unreported: This channels and time-limits constitutional litigation to a single court, an effect not apparent from the bill's child-safety framing.

gaps: The bill requires covered platforms to give safeguards to users the provider "knows" is a minor but does not require platforms to determine users' ages outside the Title I obscenity-site context.
Title I requires adult-content sites to verify age but does not specify penalties or amounts for a provider that fails to comply, relying on general FTC Act enforcement.
The Act repeatedly turns on whether a provider "knows" a user is a minor but does not define what steps establish such knowledge for platforms outside the technology-verification requirement.
The bill orders studies on chatbots, social media, and fentanyl access but does not set requirements that follow automatically from those findings.
Title IV addresses chatbot conduct toward minors but does not require chatbot providers to determine which users are minors.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bilirakis
featured_quotes.text: I rise today to speak in strong in support of H.R. 7757, the Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act, or the KIDS Act. This package will finally give parents real tools to protect their kids online. A key provision in the KIDS Act is my Kids Online Safety Act, or KOSA. I have been working on KOSA, Mr. Speaker, for 3 years, and I am proud to see it finally reach the House floor. The need for action has never been clearer.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Lee
featured_quotes.text: Children today are growing up in a digital world that looks dramatically different than it did just a generation ago. While technology has created tremendous opportunities to learn and to connect, it has also exposed young people to online predators, sexual exploitation, privacy violations, and increasingly sophisticated threats driven by artificial intelligence. Parents are doing everything they can to protect their children online but should not have to navigate these challenges alone.

added: New requirement that adult-content "covered platforms" (over one-third harmful sexual material) use technology verification measures to identify minors, effective 1 year after enactment (Title I)
New safeguards, parental tools, reporting mechanisms, and annual third-party audits for social-media-style covered platforms serving known minors (Title II Subtitle A)
New prohibitions on ephemeral messaging for known minors and direct messaging for known users under 13, plus required parental direct-messaging controls for teens (Title II Subtitle B)
New default-on communication safeguards and parental controls for online video game providers (Title III)
New disclosure, break-reminder, and content-policy requirements for AI chatbot providers serving known minors (Title IV)
New Kids Internet Safety Partnership at the Department of Commerce, sunsetting 5 years after establishment (Section 526)
New federal studies on social media use, fentanyl access, industry safety tools, and a 4-year NIH study on chatbots and minors' mental health (Title V Subtitle A)
modified: Amends the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act (15 U.S.C. 6551 et seq.) by striking sections 211 through 214 and 216 and inserting a new FTC public-awareness campaign, a 10-year annual report, and definitions (Section 522)
removed: Repeals sections 211 through 214 and 216 of the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act as they previously read (Section 522)
